@Lekanich Not sure to understand what you point out?
In the following code,  I present simplified subset of readTimeToWait code in TrafficCounter, where the time is computed:

```
bytesRecvFlowControl(size); // add the time to the "current" amount of volume to take into account
long sum = currentReadBytes.get(); // now get the data in the queue
long interval = now - lastTime.get(); // compute the time between now and last time the counter was reset
long time = (sum * 1000 / limitTraffic - interval) / 10 * 10; // compute the time to wait
```

Of course, the handler can only compute traffic shaping of what it knows, so what is already pass through this handler. 
What do you mean by "no one takes into account all the data is already waiting to be sent" ?
If the data is not sent (not reaching this handler), how do you want the handler to know about them ?

In order to ensure this handler is understodd, one has to know that this handler is only a "react" traffic shaping handler. Meaning that there is a "burst" effect in the very beginning of a transfer, mainly in receive mode (less sensitive in send mode since it can control when the data are really sent). Making the default checkInterval smaller (down limit to 100ms) tends to improve the trafficShaping but at the price of more thread activities. However in general, the default 1s is an acceptable average for most of the protocols and situations.

I suppose I don't get at all your point, so if you could give an example, it might help.

@fredericBregier Thanks for answer. I spoke about write part. Responsible for reading part separates the data normally. Some data come to channel and it is processed in handlers. ChannelTrafficShapingHandler capture data and writes some to channel and another to queue (before this we counted delay time for all pieces in the queue). And I supposed that when we count delay time for the next data we don't consider delay time of previous data (they must now be sent with a delay), and, therefore, the following data is sent along with the previous ones, although they should had to wait. Now I compared the two methods (writeTimeToWait and readTimeToWait) and found one difference in logic. This line in readTimeToWait: long lastinterval = AbstractTrafficShapingHandler.MINIMAL_WAIT; and this in writeTimeToWait: long lastinterval = AbstractTrafficShapingHandler.MINIMAL_WAIT + Math.abs(interval); It's hard to understand the fully logic of these methods for me, but can this is the reason that shaper starts to write the data too soon for large amounts of the data .

@Lekanich 
The slight difference you've seen can be safely ignored.
Indeed, to arrive to this case, the first test is wrong:

```
 if (interval > AbstractTrafficShapingHandler.MINIMAL_WAIT && sum > 0) { 
```

Which means sum is 0 (impossible since sum just get the added proposed write bytes, so in fact this test is always true) or  interval is < MINIMAL_WAIT (10ms) (keep this one in mind)
Then the second one is false again:

```
if (lastNonNullWrittenBytes > 0 && lastNonNullWrittenTime + AbstractTrafficShapingHandler.MINIMAL_WAIT < now) {
```

which means last written bytes is nul or last time accounting was done is too close to "now" (less than 10ms)

Then interval might be null or at least < 10ms (shall not be <0, but in case we compute the absolute value).
Then the lastinterval compute is 10 to 19 at most.

One can consider it is too small/ridiculous, but in practice I observed that this difference is not at all needed in Read but can improve the Write traffic shaping. Whatever, this is not significant to imply a burst of 500 MB transfer in 10s for instance if you set 1 MB of limit (so 500s).

What kind of example do you have ?
Moreover, what version do you use (since this traffic was improve/corrected in the last versions 3.9, 4.0 4.1, and Master) ?

@Lekanich 
So I understand that you set from the beginning the write and read limits, before any read/write start.
You could override doAccounting method of ChannelTrafficShapingHandler and then from there write some logs of the TraffocCounter (simpliy something like logger.warn(trafficCounter.toString())).

You could then see what is the "supposely" trafficShaping action and behavior.

I suppose of course that you send large amount of bytes using the same channel (so the ChannelTSH and not the GlobalTSH).

It would be nice too if you are able to send a test case that reproduce the behavior ?

Expected download time = 135.0. But in real life - 51sec (+/- 4 sec). I check md5 and length of the file, so I know exactly that this file loaded fully. When I put a break point when logger began to report 0 byte for a second in the method ChannelTrafficShapingHandler.sendAllValid(ChannelHandlerContext ctx), I saw more than 600 objects in queue to send (I think it's expected behavior). Yes, I use only ChannelTrafficShapingHandler. I put it first in pipeline, and set maxWaitTime to Long.MaxValue (to the waiting time was not limited to the top). The code that I use is based on the inner private framework(it's based on netty), so if I'll post an example, he will not start.

I've tested on my side, using both Global and Channel TrafficShaping with a send of 14.76 MB (write by block of 64KB), and I obtain the following traces, showing for both about 15s of transfer, while it should be aroune 14.76s (using 1024*1024 as limit).

I found out however a bug: some overriden methods are not calling the "super" corresping methods:
- in 4.0/4.1/master : handlerAdded() and handlerRemoved()
- in 3.9: channelConnected()

If you override the default class and use (in 4.0) one of those methods in your overriden implementation, that could explain the issue (the limit being not taken into account).

For your test, could you ensure that you create (for testing purpose) the ChannelTSH with the right limit from the beginning ?

Also some feedback on your comment:
 800MB in 51s means 16.5 MB/s, so roughly 131 Mbps. The logs are coherent with that (up to 22 MB/s, so 176 Mbps).
800MB with 5_1024_1024 should give 160s, so you got 1/3 of what is expected. The difference is huge, and except considering the limitation could not be applied at all, or too lately (setting the limit almost after the writes are done), I don't understand why.

Moreover, almost 180 Mbps looks like you are more hitting the "network" or "disk reading" limit, than the traffic is doing something. Does the time being the same while you have no traffic handler at all ?

Finally, the 600 objects in queue is normal since they are waiting to be sent according to the bandwidth limitation.

While I was testing using a standard code from Netty (HttpStaticFileServer), I may understand what could be the root cause.
Do you have a ChunkedWriteHandler in your Pipeline ?

A) When I change the example to not use the default ChunkedWriteHandler (so doing HttpContent by HttpContent as a piece of the file to send) : the TrafficShaping is ok
B) When I use the default example (ChunkedWriteHandler with DefaultFileRegion/HpptChunkedInput), the TrafficShaping seems bypass and the data flow as if the traffic shaping is ignore (and in fact, it is).

The pipeline is for both A and B:

```
    pipeline.addLast(new GlobalTrafficShapingHandler(ch.eventLoop(), 1024*1024, 1024*1024));
    pipeline.addLast(new HttpServerCodec());
    pipeline.addLast(new HttpObjectAggregator(65536));
    pipeline.addLast(new ChunkedWriteHandler());
    pipeline.addLast(new HttpStaticFileServerHandler());
```

I change the calculateSize() method to print the object seen (note that if objects are not of type ByteBuf or ByteBufHolder, the TrafficShaping will not work), and here is what I've got in the second cases (using default ChunkedWriteHandler):

This log shows in particular that DefaultFileRegion is passed to the last handler as is (not split into bytebuf) and therefore not recognize by the TrafficShapingHandler. Of course no traffic shaping is done at all, and the download is at maximum rate possible.

I suppose this is an internal optimization of Netty to bypass all handlers ?

I reduced the size in the last test of up to 700 megabytes (sorry, forgot to mention).
1. I set the limit values ​​at the beginning and everything is repeated again. (700MB per about 50sec)
2. In my implementation of the class I does not override any of these classes (only read(), write() and doAccounting(), last one for log).
3. And without traffic shaping 700 megabytes were loaded in 9 seconds (when I removed ChannelTrafficShapingHandler).
